Exact Attention Sensitivity and the Geometry of Transformer Stability

Seyed Morteza Emadi Affiliation: UNC-Chapel Hill, Kenan-Flagler Business School, Chapel Hill, NC, USA Correspondence to: seyed_emadi@kenan-flagler.unc.edu
Abstract

Despite powering modern AI, transformers remain mysteriously brittle to train. We develop a stability theory that explains why pre-LayerNorm works, why DeepNorm uses N−1/4N^{-1/4} scaling, and why warmup is necessary, all from first principles. Our framework has two pillars: (1) We derive the exact operator norm of the softmax Jacobian, ‖Jsoftmax​(u/τ)‖∞→1=θ⁡(p)/τ\|J_{\softmax}(u/\tau)\|_{\infty\to 1}=\theta(p)/\tau, where the balanced-mass factor θ⁡(p)∈[0,1]\theta(p)\in[0,1] quantifies attention sensitivity. (2) We introduce a block-∞\infty/RMS geometry aligned with tokenwise computation, yielding Lipschitz bounds independent of sequence length. Using this framework, we prove that pre-LN preserves identity gradient paths while post-LN compounds LayerNorm Jacobians exponentially with depth, and we show that DeepNorm’s N−1/4N^{-1/4} emerges from the quartic structure of attention’s four projection matrices. We validate our theory on 774M-parameter models and find that, contrary to the intuition that attention sharpens during training to reduce sensitivity, θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1 persists throughout. Transformer stability arises entirely from architectural gradient flow, not from attention dynamics. This finding changes how we reason about training: the architecture itself must handle sensitivity, not learned attention patterns.

Keywords: 
transformer stability, attention mechanism, Lipschitz bounds, LayerNorm, gradient flow, deep learning theory

1 Introduction

Transformers have become the dominant architecture across machine learning, powering large language models, vision systems, and multimodal applications (Vaswani et al., 2017; Touvron et al., 2023). Yet despite their empirical success, training transformers remains notoriously brittle. Loss spikes, gradient explosions, and subtle divergences can derail optimization runs that have consumed days of computation and substantial resources. The challenge intensifies with scale: deeper models and longer sequences introduce compounding instabilities that require increasingly careful hyperparameter tuning.

Practitioners manage this brittleness through a constellation of heuristics accumulated over years of empirical tuning. Pre-LayerNorm (pre-LN) architectures (Xiong et al., 2020) place normalization before attention rather than after, dramatically improving training stability for deep networks. Residual scaling rules like DeepNorm (Wang et al., 2022) multiply sublayer outputs by depth-dependent factors α≈N−1/4\alpha\approx N^{-1/4}, enabling training of 1000+ layer transformers. Learning rate warmup (Goyal et al., 2017) starts with tiny step sizes and gradually increases, preventing early-training instabilities. These techniques work, but why? What geometric or algebraic properties make pre-LN stable and post-LN unstable? Why does DeepNorm use N−1/4N^{-1/4} rather than N−1/2N^{-1/2} or N−1N^{-1}? What specifically about initialization makes warmup necessary?

This gap between practice and theory has concrete consequences. Without understanding the mechanisms that stabilize training, practitioners cannot predict which heuristics transfer to new architectures, diagnose root causes when training fails, or reason about stability from first principles. The field advances through expensive trial-and-error rather than geometric insight.

Limitations of existing theory.

Existing theoretical analyses of transformer stability fall into two camps, neither fully satisfactory.

Global worst-case analyses derive Lipschitz and smoothness bounds using ℓ2\ell_{2} or Frobenius geometry (Kim et al., 2021; Dasoulas et al., 2021). These bounds inherit spurious L\sqrt{L} factors from sequence length, suggesting that longer sequences are inherently harder to process stably. But this contradicts practice: transformers handle varying sequence lengths without corresponding stability degradation. The problem is geometric misalignment: the Frobenius norm aggregates across tokens in a way that obscures the rowwise structure of attention.

Local distribution-aware analyses focus on softmax sensitivity in isolation, deriving bounds that depend on attention sharpness (Yudin et al., 2025; Castin et al., 2024). These capture important phenomena but do not integrate cleanly into layerwise bounds for complete transformer blocks. They cannot explain why architectural choices like pre-LN vs. post-LN matter, since both use the same softmax function.

Neither approach fully explains empirical phenomena: the instability of post-LN at depth, the specific scaling factors in DeepNorm, or the geometric necessity of warmup.

Our approach: architecture-aligned geometry.

We develop a stability framework explicitly aligned with how transformers compute. The key insight is recognizing what transformers actually do at each step: LayerNorm normalizes each token independently, ignoring other tokens’ magnitudes; attention computes row-stochastic mixtures, where each output token is a convex combination of value vectors; and perturbations propagate through individual token representations, not through global sequence statistics.

These observations motivate a block-∞\infty/RMS geometry where we measure the worst-case token magnitude rather than aggregate Frobenius norms. In this geometry, attention mixing is automatically nonexpansive (convex combinations cannot increase the maximum), LayerNorm has bounded Lipschitz constant independent of input scale, and layerwise bounds depend only on architectural parameters, not on sequence length.

Contributions.

(1) Path-length exponent principle. For architectures with mm multiplicative maps in the sensitive pathway, scale each by N−1/mN^{-1/m}. Standard attention has m=4m=4, yielding DeepNorm’s N−1/4N^{-1/4}; shared WQ=WKW^{Q}=W^{K} has m=3m=3, predicting N−1/3N^{-1/3} (Theorem 6.2).

(2) Temperature warmup prediction. Our analysis predicts that temperature warmup (τhigh→τlow\tau_{\mathrm{high}}\to\tau_{\mathrm{low}}) should match learning rate warmup’s stabilization benefits by directly attenuating the 1/τ1/\tau factor in attention sensitivity, while leaving FFN gradients unthrottled (Section 6).

(3) Exact softmax sensitivity. We derive the exact operator norm ‖Jsoftmax‖∞→1=θ⁡(p)/τ\|J_{\softmax}\|_{\infty\to 1}=\theta(p)/\tau, where θ⁡(p)∈[0,1]\theta(p)\in[0,1] measures how evenly attention can be bisected. This equality (not just a bound) reveals that sensitivity depends on distribution geometry, not just temperature.

(4) Pre-LN vs post-LN mechanism. We prove pre-LN preserves an additive identity gradient path (bypassing sublayer Jacobians) while post-LN forces all gradients through LayerNorm Jacobians, causing exponential decay with depth (Theorems 5.4, 5.5).

(5) Key empirical finding. Contrary to intuition, θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1 persists throughout training; attention never sharpens to reduce sensitivity. Stability is architectural, not distributional (Section 7).

(6) Length-free layerwise bounds. Using block-∞\infty/RMS geometry, we derive Lipschitz bounds independent of sequence length (Theorem 5.1).

2 Related Work

Lipschitz analysis of attention. Kim et al. (2021) established that unconstrained self-attention is not globally Lipschitz, motivating spectral regularization approaches (Dasoulas et al., 2021; Qi et al., 2023). Recent work derives tighter local bounds by incorporating properties of the attention distribution: Yudin et al. (2025) bound the spectral norm using ordinal statistics of attention probabilities, while Castin et al. (2024) analyze smoothness under attention sharpness. We advance beyond bounds to derive the exact Jacobian norm in the ℓ∞→ℓ1\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{1} geometry and propagate it through complete layers, enabling architectural comparisons.

Normalization and deep transformers. The original transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) used post-LayerNorm, but Xiong et al. (2020) showed pre-LN dramatically improves stability for deep networks. Liu et al. (2020) connected this to gradient flow, observing that post-LN gradients can vanish or explode. We provide a precise mechanism: in pre-LN, gradients can flow directly through residual connections; in post-LN, all gradients must pass through LayerNorm at every layer, compounding across depth.

Residual scaling. DeepNorm (Wang et al., 2022) enables 1000+ layer training through careful residual scaling with α≈(2N)−1/4\alpha\approx(2N)^{-1/4} (the 22 reflects two residual sublayers per layer: MHA and FFN). Related approaches include Fixup initialization (Zhang et al., 2019) and T-Fixup (Huang et al., 2020). We derive DeepNorm’s N−1/4N^{-1/4} exponent from first principles, showing it emerges from the quartic structure of the attention pathway.

Learning rate warmup. Warmup is standard practice (Goyal et al., 2017), with explanations focusing on Adam momentum calibration (Liu et al., 2020) and loss landscape sharpness (Gilmer et al., 2022). Our analysis adds a geometric perspective: since θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1 persists throughout training, stability cannot rely on attention distributions becoming peaked; instead, warmup limits parameter updates while projection norms stabilize.

With this context, we now develop our geometric framework. We begin by introducing a norm aligned with tokenwise transformer computation, then derive exact Jacobian norms that enable architectural comparisons.

3 Geometric Framework

Analyzing transformer stability requires choosing the right geometric perspective. The choice of norm fundamentally shapes what bounds are possible and what phenomena they can capture. In this section, we argue that standard ℓ2\ell_{2}/Frobenius geometry is misaligned with transformer computation, and we introduce an alternative that respects the tokenwise structure of attention and normalization.

Notation and stability concepts.

We denote vectors x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, matrices X∈ℝL×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}, and the probability simplex ΔL−1={p∈ℝL:pi≥0,∑ipi=1}\Delta^{L-1}=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{L}:p_{i}\geq 0,\sum_{i}p_{i}=1\}. For S⊆[L]S\subseteq[L], we write p⁡(S)=∑i∈Spip(S)=\sum_{i\in S}p_{i}. We distinguish three stability concepts: layerwise Lipschitz constant Llayer=supX≠X′‖f⁡(X)−f⁡(X′)‖/‖X−X′‖L_{\text{layer}}=\sup_{X\neq X^{\prime}}\|f(X)-f(X^{\prime})\|/\|X-X^{\prime}\|, measuring local sensitivity; end-to-end sensitivity ‖∂XN/∂Xℓ‖\|\partial X_{N}/\partial X_{\ell}\|, measuring perturbation amplification across layers; and gradient flow, which describes how gradients propagate backward during backpropagation via the transposed Jacobians (∂Xℓ+1/∂Xℓ)⊤(\partial X_{\ell+1}/\partial X_{\ell})^{\top}.

3.1 Why Standard Geometry Fails

Standard Lipschitz analyses treat hidden state matrices X∈ℝL×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} as single objects, measuring perturbations in Frobenius or spectral norm. The Frobenius norm ‖Δ​X‖F=∑i,jΔ​Xi​j2\|\Delta X\|_{F}=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}\Delta X_{ij}^{2}} aggregates errors across all tokens and dimensions.

This leads to bounds that scale poorly with sequence length. Consider attention output Y=A​XY=AX where AA is row-stochastic:

‖A​X‖F≤‖A‖F​‖X‖F≤L​‖X‖F,\|AX\|_{F}\leq\|A\|_{F}\|X\|_{F}\leq\sqrt{L}\|X\|_{F},

since ‖A‖F≤L\|A\|_{F}\leq\sqrt{L} for row-stochastic AA. The L\sqrt{L} factor suggests longer sequences are inherently less stable, but this contradicts practice: transformers handle varying sequence lengths without corresponding stability degradation.

The problem is geometric misalignment. LayerNorm normalizes each token independently, ignoring other tokens’ magnitudes. Attention computes convex combinations rowwise, depending only on how value vectors are weighted, not on aggregate sequence statistics. The Frobenius norm’s global aggregation obscures this tokenwise structure.

3.2 Block-∞\infty/RMS Geometry

We adopt a norm that respects the tokenwise nature of transformer computation. All proofs for this section appear in Appendix A.

Definition 3.1 (Block-∞\infty/RMS norm).

For a matrix X=(x1,…,xL)⊤∈ℝL×dX=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{L})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} with row vectors xi∈ℝdx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define

‖X‖∞,rms=max1≤i≤L⁡‖xi‖2d.\|X\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}=\max_{1\leq i\leq L}\frac{\|x_{i}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{d}}.

Intuition.

The block-∞\infty/RMS norm asks: “What is the RMS magnitude of the worst-case token?” This respects transformer computation: LayerNorm acts on individual tokens, attention mixes tokens via convex combinations. The d\sqrt{d} normalization aligns with LayerNorm’s standard deviation: a vector with unit RMS norm satisfies 1d​∑jxj2=1\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j}x_{j}^{2}=1. Measuring worst-case token magnitude yields length-independent bounds.

Lemma 3.2 (Attention mixing is nonexpansive).

For any row-stochastic A∈ℝL×LA\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L} and V∈ℝL×dV\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}: ‖A​V‖∞,rms≤‖V‖∞,rms\|AV\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}\leq\|V\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}.

This result is central to our framework: attention mixing cannot amplify token magnitudes. Each output row is a convex combination of input rows, and convex combinations cannot exceed the maximum.

Lemma 3.3 (LayerNorm magnitude reset).

For any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, LayerNorm satisfies ‖LN⁡(x)‖rms≤‖γ‖∞+‖β‖∞\|\LN(x)\|_{\mathrm{rms}}\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}+\|\beta\|_{\infty}, where γ,β∈ℝd\gamma,\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are the learned scale and shift parameters.

This “magnitude reset” property is crucial for pre-LN stability: regardless of input magnitude, LayerNorm produces bounded output. A token with ‖x‖2=106\|x\|_{2}=10^{6} yields ‖LN⁡(x)‖rms=O⁡(1)\|\LN(x)\|_{\mathrm{rms}}=O(1). We also establish that LayerNorm has Lipschitz constant Lip⁡(LN)≤‖γ‖∞/ϵ\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}/\sqrt{\epsilon} in Appendix A, where ϵ\epsilon is the numerical stability floor.

4 Exact Softmax Sensitivity

The heart of our analysis is an exact characterization of softmax sensitivity. Unlike prior bounds that provide loose upper estimates, we derive the exact operator norm of the softmax Jacobian, revealing that sensitivity depends on a specific geometric property: the balanced-mass factor.

Before stating our main result, we introduce the quantity governing softmax sensitivity.

Definition 4.1 (Balanced-mass factor).

For a probability distribution p∈ΔL−1p\in\Delta^{L-1}, define

θ⁡(p)=4​maxS⊆[L]⁡p⁡(S)​(1−p⁡(S))∈[0,1],\theta(p)=4\max_{S\subseteq[L]}p(S)(1-p(S))\in[0,1],

where p⁡(S)=∑i∈Spip(S)=\sum_{i\in S}p_{i} is the probability mass on subset SS.

The factor θ⁡(p)\theta(p) measures how evenly probability mass can be bisected. The product p​(S)​(1−p​(S))p(S)(1-p(S)) is maximized when p⁡(S)=1/2p(S)=1/2, giving θ⁡(p)=1\theta(p)=1. It equals zero only for one-hot distributions where no subset achieves mass near 1/21/2.

Importantly, θ⁡(p)\theta(p) differs from Shannon entropy. A non-uniform distribution can still have θ=1\theta=1: for example, p=(0.4,0.1,0.4,0.1)p=(0.4,0.1,0.4,0.1) has lower entropy than uniform, but θ=1\theta=1 because p⁡({1,4})=0.5p(\{1,4\})=0.5. This distinction matters because transformers can develop structured, non-uniform attention patterns while maintaining high θ\theta, and thus high sensitivity.

With this quantity in hand, we can state our main result. We characterize softmax sensitivity using the ℓ∞→ℓ1\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{1} operator norm, where ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} on inputs measures the worst-case logit perturbation and ℓ1\ell_{1} on outputs measures total probability mass redistributed, which is precisely what matters for downstream computation.

Theorem 4.2 (Exact softmax Jacobian norm).

Let p=softmax⁡(u/τ)p=\softmax(u/\tau) for logits u∈ℝLu\in\mathbb{R}^{L} and temperature τ>0\tau>0. The softmax Jacobian J=1τ​(Diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤)J=\frac{1}{\tau}(\Diag(p)-pp^{\top}) satisfies

‖J‖∞→1=θ⁡(p)τ.\|J\|_{\infty\to 1}=\frac{\theta(p)}{\tau}.

This is an equality, not merely an upper bound. The maximum is achieved by perturbations xi=+1x_{i}=+1 for i∈S∗i\in S^{*}, xi=−1x_{i}=-1 for i∉S∗i\notin S^{*}, where S∗S^{*} achieves the maximum in the definition of θ⁡(p)\theta(p).

The intuition for this result is as follows (full proof in Appendix B). When we perturb attention logits, the softmax redistributes probability mass. The worst-case perturbation increases logits for tokens in some subset SS while decreasing logits for tokens outside SS, transferring mass across this partition. The total mass redistributed is proportional to p​(S)​(1−p​(S))p(S)(1-p(S)), which is maximized when p⁡(S)=1/2p(S)=1/2. Thus θ⁡(p)\theta(p) measures how evenly the distribution can be split in two. Unlike prior ℓ2\ell_{2} bounds that are distribution-independent (Kim et al., 2021; Castin et al., 2024; Yudin et al., 2025), our result provides an exact equality where θ⁡(p)\theta(p) captures how distribution shape determines sensitivity.

Corollary 4.3 (Sensitivity regimes).

(Proof in Appendix B.)

  1. 1.

    Uniform: p=1L​𝟏p=\frac{1}{L}\mathbf{1} gives θ⁡(p)=1\theta(p)=1 (maximum sensitivity).

  2. 2.

    One-hot: p=eip=e_{i} gives θ⁡(p)=0\theta(p)=0 (minimum sensitivity).

  3. 3.

    Peaked: If the top token has mass 1−κ1-\kappa, then θ⁡(p)≤4​κ​(1−κ)\theta(p)\leq 4\kappa(1-\kappa).

  4. 4.

    Top-kk uniform: Mass 1/k1/k on kk tokens gives θ⁡(p)=1−(1−2​⌊k/2⌋/k)2\theta(p)=1-(1-2\lfloor k/2\rfloor/k)^{2}.

The stability-expressivity trade-off.

The balanced-mass factor reveals a fundamental tension in attention design. High θ⁡(p)\theta(p) (uniform or bisectable attention) provides expressivity (the network can flexibly redistribute attention mass) but carries gradient sensitivity risk. Low θ⁡(p)\theta(p) (peaked attention) provides stability, as softmax becomes insensitive to logit perturbations, but risks entropy collapse where attention concentrates on few tokens (Dong et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2023). Our experiments show that trained transformers operate at θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1, suggesting that practical networks maintain expressivity and rely on architectural mechanisms (pre-LN identity paths, residual scaling) rather than attention sharpening for stability.

Implications for training dynamics.

Theorem 4.2 has immediate consequences for transformer training. At initialization with random weights, attention distributions are near-uniform, so θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1: the network begins in its most sensitive state. One might expect that as models learn meaningful attention patterns, distributions become peaked and θ⁡(p)\theta(p) decreases, yielding natural stabilization. However, this expectation is empirically false: our experiments (Section 7) reveal that θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1 persists throughout training. Typical transformer attention remains bisectable even after convergence, so θ⁡(p)\theta(p) functions as an approximately constant sensitivity amplifier rather than a transient initialization artifact.

This persistence has two important consequences. First, the 1/τ1/\tau scaling shows that lower temperature amplifies sensitivity, explaining why temperature tuning affects training stability. Second, since θ⁡(p)\theta(p) does not reliably decay, stability must come from controlling other factors in the attention pathway (projection norms, input magnitudes) and from architectural gradient-flow structure, rather than from attention sharpening.

The natural next question is: how does this local softmax sensitivity compound through complete transformer layers? And how do architectural choices (pre-LN vs. post-LN) affect this compounding?

5 Layerwise Stability Analysis

We now propagate the softmax sensitivity result through complete transformer layers. Let Xℓ∈ℝL×dX_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} denote the hidden state at layer ℓ\ell for ℓ=0,1,…,N\ell=0,1,\ldots,N, where NN is the total number of layers. Our goal is to understand how local sensitivity, characterized by θ⁡(p)\theta(p), combines with architectural choices to determine global stability. Proofs for this section appear in Appendix C.

5.1 Multi-Head Attention Lipschitz Bound

Multi-head attention maps input U∈ℝL×dU\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} to output MHA⁡(U)=[O1​‖⋯‖​OH]​WO\MHA(U)=[O_{1}\|\cdots\|O_{H}]W^{O}, where head hh computes:

Qh=U​WhQ,Kh=U​WhK,Vh=U​WhV,Q_{h}=UW_{h}^{Q},\quad K_{h}=UW_{h}^{K},\quad V_{h}=UW_{h}^{V},
Ah=softmax⁡(Qh​Kh⊤/(τ​dh)),Oh=Ah​Vh.A_{h}=\softmax(Q_{h}K_{h}^{\top}/(\tau\sqrt{d_{h}})),\quad O_{h}=A_{h}V_{h}.

In standard training τ=1\tau=1; we retain the explicit τ\tau to connect with our softmax sensitivity analysis and the temperature warmup proposal in Section 6. To bound the Lipschitz constant, we decompose into two pathways. The value pathway captures how input perturbations affect values VV, which are then averaged by fixed attention weights. The attention pathway captures how perturbations affect attention weights AA, which then reweight fixed values.

Theorem 5.1 (MHA Lipschitz bound).

Under the block-∞\infty/RMS norm, with input magnitude B¯U=‖U‖∞,rms​d\bar{B}_{U}=\|U\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}\sqrt{d}:

LMHA≤‖WO‖2​∑h=1H(‖WhV‖2+θ~hτ​Φh),L_{\MHA}\leq\|W^{O}\|_{2}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left(\|W_{h}^{V}\|_{2}+\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{h}}{\tau}\Phi_{h}\right),

where θ~h=maxiθ(Ah[i,:])\tilde{\theta}_{h}=\max_{i}\theta(A_{h}[i,:]) and Φh=2​B¯U2dh​‖WhQ‖2​‖WhK‖2​‖WhV‖2\Phi_{h}=\frac{2\bar{B}_{U}^{2}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\|W_{h}^{Q}\|_{2}\|W_{h}^{K}\|_{2}\|W_{h}^{V}\|_{2}. The first term ‖WhV‖2\|W_{h}^{V}\|_{2} is the value pathway contribution; the second term θ~hτ​Φh\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{h}}{\tau}\Phi_{h} is the attention pathway contribution.

Two key insights emerge. First, the bound is independent of sequence length LL; this is why we developed block-∞\infty/RMS geometry. Second, the attention pathway scales as B¯U2\bar{B}_{U}^{2}: controlling input magnitude directly controls sensitivity. The attention pathway has quartic dependence on projection norms:

θ~τ​B¯U2​‖WO‖2​‖WQ‖2​‖WK‖2​‖WV‖2.\frac{\tilde{\theta}}{\tau}\bar{B}_{U}^{2}\|W^{O}\|_{2}\|W^{Q}\|_{2}\|W^{K}\|_{2}\|W^{V}\|_{2}.

This quartic structure underlies DeepNorm’s N−1/4N^{-1/4} scaling, as we explain in Section 6.

5.2 Per-Layer Lipschitz Bounds

A natural question arises: does B¯U\bar{B}_{U} (the MHA input magnitude) remain bounded as we go deeper? This depends on architecture. We now show that both pre-LN and post-LN have bounded per-layer Lipschitz constants, but the difference between them lies elsewhere.

Throughout this section, we write Lip⁡(LN)\mathrm{Lip}(\LN) for the Lipschitz constant of LayerNorm. By Lemma A.1, Lip⁡(LN)≤‖γ‖∞/ϵ\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}/\sqrt{\epsilon}, which depends only on the scale parameter γ\gamma and numerical stability constant ϵ\epsilon.

Pre-LN architecture.

In pre-LN, normalization precedes each sublayer:

Xℓ+1=Xℓ+MHA⁡(LN⁡(Xℓ)).X_{\ell+1}=X_{\ell}+\MHA(\LN(X_{\ell})).

The MHA receives U=LN⁡(Xℓ)U=\LN(X_{\ell}) as input. By Lemma 3.3, ‖U‖∞,rms≤‖γ‖∞+‖β‖∞\|U\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}+\|\beta\|_{\infty} regardless of how large XℓX_{\ell} grows. The residual stream XℓX_{\ell} can accumulate unboundedly across layers, but the LayerNorm before MHA acts as a magnitude barrier: it resets the input to a bounded range at every layer. This structural guarantee ensures B¯U\bar{B}_{U} is bounded independently of layer depth.

Post-LN architecture.

In post-LN, normalization follows each sublayer:

Xℓ+1=LN⁡(Xℓ+MHA⁡(Xℓ)).X_{\ell+1}=\LN(X_{\ell}+\MHA(X_{\ell})).

The MHA receives XℓX_{\ell} directly. However, for ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, XℓX_{\ell} is the output of the previous layer’s LayerNorm, so ‖Xℓ‖∞,rms≤‖γ‖∞+‖β‖∞\|X_{\ell}\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}+\|\beta\|_{\infty} by Lemma 3.3. Thus post-LN also has bounded B¯U\bar{B}_{U}, but this is a consequential property (each layer’s output happens to be normalized) rather than a structural guarantee (we don’t explicitly normalize before MHA). Since LMHAL_{\MHA} depends on B¯U2\bar{B}_{U}^{2} through the attention pathway (Theorem 5.1), both mechanisms yield bounded LMHAL_{\MHA}. The pre-LN bounding mechanism is more robust to architectural modifications because it provides a structural guarantee rather than relying on the output of the previous layer. We now state the complete per-layer bounds.

Theorem 5.2 (Pre-LN: full layer bound).

A complete pre-LN layer (MHA + FFN sublayers) has Lipschitz constant

Llayerpre≤(1+Lip⁡(LN)⋅LMHA)​(1+Lip⁡(LN)⋅LFFN),L_{\mathrm{layer}}^{\mathrm{pre}}\leq(1+\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\cdot L_{\MHA})(1+\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\cdot L_{\FFN}),

which depends only on weight norms, LayerNorm parameters, and architectural constants. It is independent of layer index ℓ\ell, depth NN, and sequence length LL.

Theorem 5.3 (Post-LN: full layer bound).

A complete post-LN layer has Lipschitz constant

Llayerpost≤Lip​(LN)2​(1+LMHA)​(1+LFFN),L_{\mathrm{layer}}^{\mathrm{post}}\leq\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)^{2}(1+L_{\MHA})(1+L_{\FFN}),

which is also independent of ℓ\ell, NN, and LL.

The key observation is that both architectures have bounded per-layer Lipschitz constants. Each layer, viewed in isolation, behaves similarly. If per-layer behavior were all that mattered, pre-LN and post-LN would be equivalent. The difference must lie in how layers compose, specifically in gradient flow.

5.3 Gradient Flow Analysis

We now examine how gradients propagate through depth. This is where pre-LN and post-LN fundamentally differ. Let JMHA​(X)J_{\MHA}(X) and JLN​(Y)J_{\LN}(Y) denote the Jacobians of MHA and LayerNorm evaluated at inputs XX and YY, respectively. The layer Jacobian ∂Xℓ+1/∂Xℓ\partial X_{\ell+1}/\partial X_{\ell} determines how gradients flow backward through layer ℓ\ell.

Pre-LN gradient structure.

In pre-LN, Xℓ+1=Xℓ+MHA⁡(LN⁡(Xℓ))X_{\ell+1}=X_{\ell}+\MHA(\LN(X_{\ell})), so the layer Jacobian is:

∂Xℓ+1∂Xℓ=I+JMHA​(LN⁡(Xℓ))⋅JLN​(Xℓ).\frac{\partial X_{\ell+1}}{\partial X_{\ell}}=I+J_{\MHA}(\LN(X_{\ell}))\cdot J_{\LN}(X_{\ell}).

The identity II appears as an additive term.

Theorem 5.4 (Pre-LN: identity gradient path).

Define Jk:=JMHA​(LN⁡(Xk))⋅JLN​(Xk)J_{k}:=J_{\MHA}(\LN(X_{k}))\cdot J_{\LN}(X_{k}). Then:

  1. (i)

    Each sublayer Jacobian is bounded: ‖Jk‖≤LMHA⋅Lip⁡(LN)=:C\|J_{k}\|\leq L_{\MHA}\cdot\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)=:C, independent of kk, NN, and LL.

  2. (ii)

    The end-to-end Jacobian expands as:

    ∂Xm∂Xℓ=∏k=ℓm−1(I+Jk)=I+∑k=ℓm−1Jk+O⁡(‖J‖2).\frac{\partial X_{m}}{\partial X_{\ell}}=\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}(I+J_{k})=I+\sum_{k=\ell}^{m-1}J_{k}+O(\|J\|^{2}).
  3. (iii)

    The identity term provides a direct gradient pathway: gradients can flow through the residual connection without passing through sublayer Jacobians JkJ_{k}.

Part (iii) is the key stability insight: pre-LN provides an explicit skip pathway (the Jacobian contains II additively), so gradients are never forced through LayerNorm at every layer. This structural difference, not a quantitative bound, is why pre-LN trains more stably than post-LN.

Post-LN gradient structure.

In post-LN, Xℓ+1=LN⁡(Xℓ+MHA⁡(Xℓ))X_{\ell+1}=\LN(X_{\ell}+\MHA(X_{\ell})), so the LayerNorm Jacobian appears on the outside:

∂Xℓ+1∂Xℓ=JLN​(Yℓ)⋅(I+JMHA​(Xℓ)),\frac{\partial X_{\ell+1}}{\partial X_{\ell}}=J_{\LN}(Y_{\ell})\cdot(I+J_{\MHA}(X_{\ell})),

where Yℓ=Xℓ+MHA⁡(Xℓ)Y_{\ell}=X_{\ell}+\MHA(X_{\ell}).

Theorem 5.5 (Post-LN: no identity gradient path).

The end-to-end Jacobian is:

  1. (i)

    ∂Xm∂Xℓ=∏k=ℓm−1JLN​(Yk)​(I+JMHA​(Xk))\displaystyle\frac{\partial X_{m}}{\partial X_{\ell}}=\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}J_{\LN}(Y_{k})(I+J_{\MHA}(X_{k})).

  2. (ii)

    The LayerNorm Jacobian JLN​(y)J_{\LN}(y) is projection-like: it annihilates the constant direction (JLN​(y)​𝟏=0J_{\LN}(y)\mathbf{1}=0) and contracts variance.

  3. (iii)

    Expanding the product yields ∏k=ℓm−1JLN​(Yk)+terms involving ​JMHA\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}J_{\LN}(Y_{k})+\text{terms involving }J_{\MHA}. There is no additive identity term.

The absence of an identity path is critical: unlike pre-LN where the Jacobian contains an additive II term, here every gradient path passes through LayerNorm Jacobians at each layer. Since JLNJ_{\LN} is projection-like (contractive in certain directions), the product of these operators causes gradients along certain directions to decay exponentially with depth. This is why deep post-LN transformers are difficult to train without careful initialization.

5.4 Discussion

Both architectures have bounded per-layer Lipschitz constants; the critical difference is gradient flow structure. Pre-LN preserves an additive identity path (gradients can bypass sublayer Jacobians), while post-LN forces all gradients through LayerNorm Jacobians at every layer, causing exponential decay along contracted directions.

6 From Geometry to Practice

We now apply our geometric framework to explain widely-used training heuristics, including residual scaling (DeepNorm) and learning rate warmup, and derive a general path-length exponent principle for stabilizing novel architectures. Proofs for this section appear in Appendix D.

6.1 Residual Scaling and the N−1/4N^{-1/4} Exponent

DeepNet (Wang et al., 2022) introduces DeepNorm, a normalization scheme that stabilizes deep post-LN transformers by scaling residual contributions:

Xℓ+1=LN⁡(Xℓ+α⋅MHA⁡(Xℓ))X_{\ell+1}=\LN(X_{\ell}+\alpha\cdot\MHA(X_{\ell}))

with α≈(2N)−1/4\alpha\approx(2N)^{-1/4}, enabling training of 1000+ layer transformers. Why N−1/4N^{-1/4}, rather than N−1/2N^{-1/2} or N−1N^{-1}?

The answer lies in the quartic structure of the attention pathway identified in Theorem 5.1. Recall that the attention-pathway contribution to the MHA Lipschitz constant scales as:

θ~τ⋅B¯U2⋅‖WO‖2​‖WQ‖2​‖WK‖2​‖WV‖2.\frac{\tilde{\theta}}{\tau}\cdot\bar{B}_{U}^{2}\cdot\|W^{O}\|_{2}\|W^{Q}\|_{2}\|W^{K}\|_{2}\|W^{V}\|_{2}.

This is the only pathway containing the softmax Jacobian, and it depends multiplicatively on four projection matrices.

Theorem 6.1 (Projection scaling for transformers).

Suppose the four attention projections have comparable operator norms: ‖WQ‖2∼‖WK‖2∼‖WV‖2∼‖WO‖2∼β\|W^{Q}\|_{2}\sim\|W^{K}\|_{2}\sim\|W^{V}\|_{2}\sim\|W^{O}\|_{2}\sim\beta. The attention-pathway contribution to each layer’s Lipschitz constant scales as β4\beta^{4}. For controlled depth compounding, defined as per-layer contribution O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) so that the NN-layer product remains O⁡(1)O(1), we require:

β4=O(1/N)⟹β=O(N−1/4).\beta^{4}=O(1/N)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\beta=O(N^{-1/4}).

The N−1/4N^{-1/4} exponent emerges directly from the fact that four matrices appear multiplicatively in the sensitive pathway. This is a structural property of attention, not an empirical coincidence.

Connection to DeepNorm.

DeepNorm implements this scaling in two complementary ways: (1) initialization scaling of attention projection matrices, reducing ‖WQ‖2,‖WK‖2,‖WV‖2,‖WO‖2\|W^{Q}\|_{2},\|W^{K}\|_{2},\|W^{V}\|_{2},\|W^{O}\|_{2} jointly by a depth-dependent factor; and (2) an explicit residual multiplier α\alpha providing additional control. Both mechanisms target the quartic term. The empirical choice α≈(2N)−1/4\alpha\approx(2N)^{-1/4} matches our theoretical prediction exactly.

6.2 The Path-Length Exponent Principle: A Design Rule

The analysis of DeepNorm reveals a general design rule for deep architectures.

Theorem 6.2 (Path-length exponent principle).

Consider a deep network with NN layers where the dominant sensitivity pathway at each layer depends multiplicatively on mm linear maps with comparable operator norms β\beta. The per-layer sensitivity contribution scales as βm\beta^{m}. For controlled depth compounding (total sensitivity O⁡(1)O(1) as N→∞N\to\infty), the scaling per map must satisfy:

βm=O(1/N)⟹β=O(N−1/m).\beta^{m}=O(1/N)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\beta=O(N^{-1/m}).

This principle makes testable predictions. Standard attention (m=4m=4) requires N−1/4N^{-1/4}, matching DeepNorm’s empirical (2N)−1/4(2N)^{-1/4} exactly. The principle predicts for other architectures: shared WQ=WKW^{Q}=W^{K} designs (m=3m=3) require N−1/3N^{-1/3}; linear attention (m=2m=2) requires N−1/2N^{-1/2}.

Actionable guidance: To stabilize a novel deep architecture, identify the dominant sensitivity pathway, count the multiplicative maps mm, and scale each by N−1/mN^{-1/m}.

6.3 Learning Rate Warmup

Warmup is standard practice for transformer training (Goyal et al., 2017), with existing explanations focusing on Adam momentum calibration (Liu et al., 2020) and loss landscape sharpness (Gilmer et al., 2022). Our framework suggests a different mechanism. Given that θ⁡(p)\theta(p) characterizes softmax sensitivity (Section 4), one might hypothesize that warmup protects during an early phase when attention is uniform and thus maximally sensitive (θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1), with stability emerging as attention sharpens (θ⁡(p)→0\theta(p)\to 0). However, our experiments (Section 7) refute this: θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1 persists throughout training.

Since θ⁡(p)\theta(p) does not decay, warmup cannot function by waiting for attention to sharpen. Instead, consider the full attention-pathway sensitivity from Theorem 5.1:

θ~τ⋅B¯U2⋅‖WO‖2​‖WQ‖2​‖WK‖2​‖WV‖2.\frac{\tilde{\theta}}{\tau}\cdot\bar{B}_{U}^{2}\cdot\|W^{O}\|_{2}\|W^{Q}\|_{2}\|W^{K}\|_{2}\|W^{V}\|_{2}.

While θ~/τ≈1/τ\tilde{\theta}/\tau\approx 1/\tau remains constant, the other factors change rapidly in early training: projection norms drift from initialization, LayerNorm scale parameters adapt, and optimizer moment estimates calibrate. This makes early training the period of greatest vulnerability to the gradient compounding identified in Theorem 5.5.

Warmup functions as sensitivity throttling: by limiting parameter updates during the high-drift early phase, it prevents runaway growth of multiplicative sensitivity factors before the network enters a better-conditioned regime. Our framework predicts that temperature warmup (τinit>τfinal\tau_{\mathrm{init}}>\tau_{\mathrm{final}}, decaying over warmup steps) should provide equivalent stabilization by directly attenuating 1/τ1/\tau. Crucially, temperature warmup targets only the attention pathway, leaving FFN and embedding gradients unthrottled, potentially enabling faster early optimization of non-attention parameters.

7 Empirical Verification

We validate our theoretical framework through experiments on 774M-parameter GPT-2-style transformers trained on FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024). Models have d=1280d=1280, N=36N=36 layers, H=20H=20 heads, and context length L=1024L=1024. Training uses AdamW with learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, 500-step linear warmup, cosine decay, and gradient clipping at norm 1.0. We report results across 3 random seeds. Full experimental details appear in Appendix E.

Theorem verification.

We verify Theorem 4.2 by independently computing both sides of ‖Jsoftmax‖∞→1=θ⁡(p)/τ\|J_{\softmax}\|_{\infty\to 1}=\theta(p)/\tau for 500 random distributions at each sequence length L∈{8,…,1024}L\in\{8,\ldots,1024\}. The identity holds to machine precision (relative error <10−13<10^{-13}); see Appendix E for details.

Training dynamics.

Figure 1 presents the core comparison. The top-left panel shows Pre-LN achieves stable convergence to loss 51.5, while Post-LN plateaus at 60.6 with a volatile trajectory. The top-right panel reveals the mechanism: Post-LN experiences a gradient spike at step 2400 reaching 5×5\times the clipping threshold, while Pre-LN maintains smooth gradient flow.

Persistence of θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1.

The bottom-left panel provides a central finding: in our 774M-parameter GPT-2-style experiments on FineWeb, θ⁡(p)/τ\theta(p)/\tau remains exactly 1.0 throughout training for both architectures. This rules out attention sharpening as an explanation for stability differences: both architectures operate at maximal softmax sensitivity. The stability gap arises entirely from gradient flow structure, not from attention becoming peaked. We confirm θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1 holds across all layers in Appendix E. Note that θ⁡(p)\theta(p) measures bisectability, not uniformity: even a sparse top-kk distribution maintains θ≈1\theta\approx 1 if the top tokens can be partitioned to sum near 0.50.5. Only near-one-hot attention (one token dominating) drives θ\theta toward zero.

Layer-wise gradient pathology.

The bottom-right panel validates Theorem 5.5. Pre-LN shows gradient norms varying smoothly across layers, consistent with the identity path preserving gradient magnitude. Post-LN exhibits the predicted pathology: gradients vanish to near-zero for layers 1–30, then spike at output layers. This is the compounding effect of LayerNorm Jacobians our theory identifies. This pattern reconciles the apparent tension between our theory (gradient decay through depth) and the observed gradient spikes: the overall gradient norm is dominated by output-layer contributions, while early layers receive insufficient gradient signal to update effectively.

Warmup validation.

Since θ⁡(p)/τ=1\theta(p)/\tau=1 throughout, warmup cannot function by waiting for attention to sharpen. Figure 2 shows the projection norm product Gℓ=‖WO‖2​‖WQ‖2​‖WK‖2​‖WV‖2G_{\ell}=\|W^{O}\|_{2}\|W^{Q}\|_{2}\|W^{K}\|_{2}\|W^{V}\|_{2} grows substantially during training (approximately 3×3\times in log scale). Crucially, the steepest growth occurs after warmup completes, validating our interpretation: warmup limits parameter updates during the early phase when these multiplicative factors would otherwise grow most rapidly.

8 Conclusion

We developed a geometric stability theory for transformers built on two foundations: the exact softmax sensitivity identity ‖Jsoftmax‖∞→1=θ⁡(p)/τ\|J_{\softmax}\|_{\infty\to 1}=\theta(p)/\tau and a block-∞\infty/RMS geometry that yields sequence-length-independent bounds. Our framework explains why pre-LN preserves identity gradient paths while post-LN compounds LayerNorm Jacobians, why DeepNorm uses N−1/4N^{-1/4} scaling (four multiplicative projections), and why warmup functions as sensitivity throttling rather than waiting for attention to sharpen.

Key finding: θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1 persists throughout training; attention never sharpens to reduce sensitivity. Transformer stability arises entirely from architectural gradient flow, not learned attention patterns.

Actionable guidance:

  • •

    Design rule: Count multiplicative maps mm in the sensitivity pathway; scale each by N−1/mN^{-1/m}. Standard attention has m=4m=4; shared WQ=WKW^{Q}=W^{K} has m=3m=3.

  • •

    Training rule: Temperature warmup (τhigh→τlow\tau_{\mathrm{high}}\to\tau_{\mathrm{low}}) should substitute for LR warmup; it targets attention directly while preserving FFN gradients.

  • •

    Architecture rule: Pre-LN provides an additive identity gradient path; post-LN forces gradients through LayerNorm at every layer, requiring DeepNorm-style compensation.

  • •

    Do not rely on attention sharpening for stability: θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1 persists throughout training.

Limitations. Our bounds are worst-case; predicting precise learning rates remains open. Experimental validation of temperature warmup and N−1/mN^{-1/m} scaling for m≠4m\neq 4 are natural next steps. Extensions to RMSNorm and MoE would broaden applicability.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

Proof of Lemma 3.3 (LayerNorm magnitude reset).

LayerNorm computes

LN⁡(x)=γ⊙x−μ⁡(x)​𝟏σ⁡(x)+β,\LN(x)=\gamma\odot\frac{x-\mu(x)\mathbf{1}}{\sigma(x)}+\beta,

where μ⁡(x)=1d​∑j=1dxj\mu(x)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_{j}, σ⁡(x)=1d​∑j=1d(xj−μ⁡(x))2+ϵ\sigma(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_{j}-\mu(x))^{2}+\epsilon}, and 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the all-ones vector.

‖x^‖22=∑j=1dx^j2=∑j=1d(xj−μ⁡(x))2σ​(x)2=d⋅(σ​(x)2−ϵ)σ​(x)2≤d.\|\hat{x}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\hat{x}_{j}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{(x_{j}-\mu(x))^{2}}{\sigma(x)^{2}}=\frac{d\cdot(\sigma(x)^{2}-\epsilon)}{\sigma(x)^{2}}\leq d.

Similarly, ‖β‖2≤‖β‖∞​d\|\beta\|_{2}\leq\|\beta\|_{\infty}\sqrt{d}. Therefore:

‖LN⁡(x)‖rms≤‖γ‖∞​d+‖β‖∞​dd=‖γ‖∞+‖β‖∞.\|\LN(x)\|_{\mathrm{rms}}\leq\frac{\|\gamma\|_{\infty}\sqrt{d}+\|\beta\|_{\infty}\sqrt{d}}{\sqrt{d}}=\|\gamma\|_{\infty}+\|\beta\|_{\infty}.

Lemma A.1 (LayerNorm Lipschitz constant).

The Lipschitz constant of LayerNorm satisfies Lip⁡(LN)≤‖γ‖∞/ϵ\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}/\sqrt{\epsilon}, where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is the numerical stability floor in the denominator.

Proof.

The Jacobian of LayerNorm at xx is

JLN​(x)=Diag⁡(γ)σ⁡(x)​(I−𝟏𝟏⊤d−(x−μ​𝟏)​(x−μ​𝟏)⊤d​σ​(x)2),J_{\LN}(x)=\frac{\Diag(\gamma)}{\sigma(x)}\left(I-\frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}}{d}-\frac{(x-\mu\mathbf{1})(x-\mu\mathbf{1})^{\top}}{d\sigma(x)^{2}}\right),

where μ=μ⁡(x)\mu=\mu(x) for brevity. Let Pμ=I−𝟏𝟏⊤dP_{\mu}=I-\frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}}{d} be the projection onto the orthogonal complement of 𝟏\mathbf{1}, and let x^=(x−μ⁡(x)​𝟏)/σ⁡(x)\hat{x}=(x-\mu(x)\mathbf{1})/\sigma(x) be the normalized centered vector. Then:

Appendix B Proof of Theorem 4.2: Exact Softmax Jacobian Norm

This appendix provides the proof of Theorem 4.2 from Section 4, which establishes the exact ℓ∞→ℓ1\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{1} operator norm of the softmax Jacobian.

Proof of Theorem 4.2.

The ℓ∞→ℓ1\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{1} operator norm is ‖J‖∞→1=max‖x‖∞≤1⁡‖J​x‖1\|J\|_{\infty\to 1}=\max_{\|x\|_{\infty}\leq 1}\|Jx\|_{1}. Since ‖J​x‖1\|Jx\|_{1} is a convex function of xx and the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} ball is a polytope, the maximum is achieved at a vertex, i.e., at some x∈{±1}Lx\in\{\pm 1\}^{L}.

For any vertex xx, let S={i:xi=+1}S=\{i:x_{i}=+1\} denote the positive indices and S¯=[L]∖S\bar{S}=[L]\setminus S the negative indices. Define

α=p⊤​x=∑i∈Spi−∑i∈S¯pi=p⁡(S)−(1−p⁡(S))=2​p​(S)−1.\alpha=p^{\top}x=\sum_{i\in S}p_{i}-\sum_{i\in\bar{S}}p_{i}=p(S)-(1-p(S))=2p(S)-1.

The Jacobian J=1τ​(Diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤)J=\frac{1}{\tau}(\Diag(p)-pp^{\top}) acts on xx as:

(J​x)i=1τ​(pi​xi−pi​(p⊤​x))=piτ​(xi−α).(Jx)_{i}=\frac{1}{\tau}\left(p_{i}x_{i}-p_{i}(p^{\top}x)\right)=\frac{p_{i}}{\tau}(x_{i}-\alpha).

We compute (J​x)i(Jx)_{i} separately for each case:

  • •

    For i∈Si\in S: xi=+1x_{i}=+1, so (J​x)i=piτ​(1−α)=piτ​(1−(2​p​(S)−1))=2​piτ​(1−p⁡(S))(Jx)_{i}=\frac{p_{i}}{\tau}(1-\alpha)=\frac{p_{i}}{\tau}(1-(2p(S)-1))=\frac{2p_{i}}{\tau}(1-p(S)).

  • •

    For i∈S¯i\in\bar{S}: xi=−1x_{i}=-1, so (J​x)i=piτ​(−1−α)=piτ​(−1−(2​p​(S)−1))=−2​piτ​p​(S)(Jx)_{i}=\frac{p_{i}}{\tau}(-1-\alpha)=\frac{p_{i}}{\tau}(-1-(2p(S)-1))=\frac{-2p_{i}}{\tau}p(S).

Since p⁡(S)∈[0,1]p(S)\in[0,1], we have α=2​p​(S)−1∈[−1,1]\alpha=2p(S)-1\in[-1,1]. This ensures (1−α)≥0(1-\alpha)\geq 0 and (1+α)≥0(1+\alpha)\geq 0, so the signs are determined by the subset membership. Computing the ℓ1\ell_{1} norm:

‖J​x‖1\displaystyle\|Jx\|_{1} =∑i∈S|2​piτ​(1−p⁡(S))|+∑i∈S¯|−2​piτ​p​(S)|\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in S}\left|\frac{2p_{i}}{\tau}(1-p(S))\right|+\sum_{i\in\bar{S}}\left|\frac{-2p_{i}}{\tau}p(S)\right|
=2​(1−p​(S))τ​∑i∈Spi+2​p​(S)τ​∑i∈S¯pi\displaystyle=\frac{2(1-p(S))}{\tau}\sum_{i\in S}p_{i}+\frac{2p(S)}{\tau}\sum_{i\in\bar{S}}p_{i}
=2​(1−p​(S))τ⋅p⁡(S)+2​p​(S)τ⋅(1−p⁡(S))\displaystyle=\frac{2(1-p(S))}{\tau}\cdot p(S)+\frac{2p(S)}{\tau}\cdot(1-p(S))
=4τ​p​(S)​(1−p⁡(S)).\displaystyle=\frac{4}{\tau}p(S)(1-p(S)).

Since vertices x∈{±1}Lx\in\{\pm 1\}^{L} correspond bijectively to subsets S⊆[L]S\subseteq[L], maximizing over all vertices is equivalent to maximizing over all subsets:

‖J‖∞→1\displaystyle\|J\|_{\infty\to 1} =maxS⊆[L]⁡4τ​p​(S)​(1−p⁡(S))\displaystyle=\max_{S\subseteq[L]}\frac{4}{\tau}p(S)(1-p(S))

The bound is achieved exactly. Let S∗S^{*} be any subset achieving the maximum in the definition of θ⁡(p)\theta(p), and define x∗∈{±1}Lx^{*}\in\{\pm 1\}^{L} by xi∗=+1x^{*}_{i}=+1 if i∈S∗i\in S^{*} and xi∗=−1x^{*}_{i}=-1 otherwise. Then ‖x∗‖∞=1\|x^{*}\|_{\infty}=1 and

Remark B.1 (Connection to total variation).

The ℓ1\ell_{1} norm of the output ‖J​x‖1\|Jx\|_{1} equals twice the total variation distance between the perturbed and original distributions (to first order). The worst-case perturbation x∗x^{*} identifies the optimal bisection of probability mass, maximizing redistribution under bounded logit changes.

Remark B.2 (Comparison to ℓ2\ell_{2} bounds).

Prior work established ‖Jsoftmax‖2→2≤1/(2​τ)\|J_{\softmax}\|_{2\to 2}\leq 1/(2\tau) (Kim et al., 2021), a distribution-independent bound. Our result is stronger in two respects: it is an exact equality (not an upper bound), and the balanced-mass factor θ⁡(p)\theta(p) captures how the distribution shape modulates sensitivity.

Appendix C Proofs for Section 5: Layerwise Stability

This appendix provides proofs for the layerwise stability results in Section 5. We organize the proofs to follow the main text: first the MHA Lipschitz bound, then per-layer Lipschitz bounds for both architectures, and finally gradient flow analysis.

C.2 Proof of Theorem 5.2: Pre-LN Full Layer Bound

Proof.

A complete pre-LN transformer layer consists of two sublayers:

Zℓ\displaystyle Z_{\ell} =Xℓ+MHA⁡(LN⁡(Xℓ)),\displaystyle=X_{\ell}+\MHA(\LN(X_{\ell})),
Xℓ+1\displaystyle X_{\ell+1} =Zℓ+FFN⁡(LN⁡(Zℓ)).\displaystyle=Z_{\ell}+\FFN(\LN(Z_{\ell})).

Bounded input magnitude.

In pre-LN, the MHA sublayer receives input U=LN⁡(Xℓ)U=\LN(X_{\ell}). By Lemma 3.3:

‖LN⁡(Xℓ)‖∞,rms≤‖γ‖∞+‖β‖∞\|\LN(X_{\ell})\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}+\|\beta\|_{\infty}

for any input XℓX_{\ell}, regardless of ‖Xℓ‖∞,rms\|X_{\ell}\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}. Thus the MHA input magnitude is:

B¯U=‖U‖∞,rms​d≤(‖γ‖∞+‖β‖∞)​d,\bar{B}_{U}=\|U\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}\sqrt{d}\leq(\|\gamma\|_{\infty}+\|\beta\|_{\infty})\sqrt{d},

which is independent of layer index ℓ\ell, total depth NN, sequence length LL, and residual stream magnitude ‖Xℓ‖\|X_{\ell}\|.

MHA sublayer.

The map Xℓ↦Zℓ=Xℓ+MHA⁡(LN⁡(Xℓ))X_{\ell}\mapsto Z_{\ell}=X_{\ell}+\MHA(\LN(X_{\ell})) has Lipschitz constant:

LMHA−sub≤1+Lip(MHA∘LN)≤1+LMHA⋅Lip(LN).L_{\mathrm{MHA-sub}}\leq 1+\mathrm{Lip}(\MHA\circ\LN)\leq 1+L_{\MHA}\cdot\mathrm{Lip}(\LN).

FFN sublayer.

The map Zℓ↦Xℓ+1=Zℓ+FFN⁡(LN⁡(Zℓ))Z_{\ell}\mapsto X_{\ell+1}=Z_{\ell}+\FFN(\LN(Z_{\ell})) has Lipschitz constant:

LFFN−sub≤1+LFFN⋅Lip⁡(LN).L_{\mathrm{FFN-sub}}\leq 1+L_{\FFN}\cdot\mathrm{Lip}(\LN).

The FFN Lipschitz constant LFFNL_{\FFN} for a standard two-layer network FFN⁡(x)=W2​σ​(W1​x+b1)+b2\FFN(x)=W_{2}\sigma(W_{1}x+b_{1})+b_{2} with 1-Lipschitz activation σ\sigma (e.g., ReLU) satisfies LFFN≤‖W2‖2​‖W1‖2L_{\FFN}\leq\|W_{2}\|_{2}\|W_{1}\|_{2}, which depends only on weight norms.

Full layer.

The composition has Lipschitz constant:

Llayerpre\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{layer}}^{\mathrm{pre}} ≤LMHA−sub⋅LFFN−sub\displaystyle\leq L_{\mathrm{MHA-sub}}\cdot L_{\mathrm{FFN-sub}}
=(1+Lip⁡(LN)⋅LMHA)​(1+Lip⁡(LN)⋅LFFN).\displaystyle=(1+\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\cdot L_{\MHA})(1+\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\cdot L_{\FFN}).

Since B¯U\bar{B}_{U} is bounded independently of ℓ\ell, NN, LL, Theorem 5.1 implies LMHAL_{\MHA} is also independent of these quantities. By Lemma A.1, Lip⁡(LN)≤‖γ‖∞/ϵ\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}/\sqrt{\epsilon} depends only on LayerNorm parameters.

Therefore LlayerpreL_{\mathrm{layer}}^{\mathrm{pre}} depends only on weight norms, LayerNorm parameters, and architectural constants. It is independent of layer index ℓ\ell, total depth NN, and sequence length LL. ∎

C.3 Proof of Theorem 5.3: Post-LN Full Layer Bound

Proof.

A complete post-LN transformer layer consists of two sublayers:

Zℓ\displaystyle Z_{\ell} =LN⁡(Xℓ+MHA⁡(Xℓ)),\displaystyle=\LN(X_{\ell}+\MHA(X_{\ell})),
Xℓ+1\displaystyle X_{\ell+1} =LN⁡(Zℓ+FFN⁡(Zℓ)).\displaystyle=\LN(Z_{\ell}+\FFN(Z_{\ell})).

Input magnitude analysis.

In post-LN, the input XℓX_{\ell} to layer ℓ\ell is the output of the LayerNorm from layer ℓ−1\ell-1. By Lemma 3.3:

‖Xℓ‖∞,rms≤‖γ‖∞+‖β‖∞.\|X_{\ell}\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}+\|\beta\|_{\infty}.

Thus B¯U=‖Xℓ‖∞,rms​d≤(‖γ‖∞+‖β‖∞)​d\bar{B}_{U}=\|X_{\ell}\|_{\infty,\mathrm{rms}}\sqrt{d}\leq(\|\gamma\|_{\infty}+\|\beta\|_{\infty})\sqrt{d}, and by Theorem 5.1, LMHAL_{\MHA} is bounded independently of ℓ\ell, NN, LL.

MHA sublayer.

The map Xℓ↦Zℓ=LN⁡(Xℓ+MHA⁡(Xℓ))X_{\ell}\mapsto Z_{\ell}=\LN(X_{\ell}+\MHA(X_{\ell})) has Lipschitz constant:

LMHA−sub≤Lip⁡(LN)⋅(1+LMHA).L_{\mathrm{MHA-sub}}\leq\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\cdot(1+L_{\MHA}).

FFN sublayer.

The map Zℓ↦Xℓ+1=LN⁡(Zℓ+FFN⁡(Zℓ))Z_{\ell}\mapsto X_{\ell+1}=\LN(Z_{\ell}+\FFN(Z_{\ell})) has Lipschitz constant:

LFFN−sub≤Lip⁡(LN)⋅(1+LFFN).L_{\mathrm{FFN-sub}}\leq\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\cdot(1+L_{\FFN}).

Full layer.

The composition has Lipschitz constant:

Llayerpost\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{layer}}^{\mathrm{post}} ≤LMHA−sub⋅LFFN−sub\displaystyle\leq L_{\mathrm{MHA-sub}}\cdot L_{\mathrm{FFN-sub}}
=Lip​(LN)2​(1+LMHA)​(1+LFFN).\displaystyle=\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)^{2}(1+L_{\MHA})(1+L_{\FFN}).

This depends only on weight norms, LayerNorm parameters, and architectural constants. It is independent of ℓ\ell, NN, and LL. ∎

C.4 Proof of Theorem 5.4: Pre-LN Identity Gradient Path

Proof.

We prove each part in sequence.

Part (i): Bounded sublayer Jacobian.

The pre-LN layer computes Xℓ+1=Xℓ+MHA⁡(LN⁡(Xℓ))X_{\ell+1}=X_{\ell}+\MHA(\LN(X_{\ell})). By the chain rule, the layer Jacobian is I+JkI+J_{k} where Jk:=JMHA​(LN⁡(Xk))⋅JLN​(Xk)J_{k}:=J_{\MHA}(\LN(X_{k}))\cdot J_{\LN}(X_{k}).

By Theorem 5.2, LMHAL_{\MHA} is bounded independently of kk, NN, and LL. By Lemma A.1, Lip⁡(LN)≤‖γ‖∞/ϵ\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)\leq\|\gamma\|_{\infty}/\sqrt{\epsilon}. Therefore:

‖Jk‖≤LMHA⋅Lip⁡(LN)=:C,\|J_{k}\|\leq L_{\MHA}\cdot\mathrm{Lip}(\LN)=:C,

where CC is a constant independent of kk, NN, and LL.

Part (ii): End-to-end Jacobian expansion.

For ℓ<m\ell<m:

∂Xm∂Xℓ=∏k=ℓm−1∂Xk+1∂Xk=∏k=ℓm−1(I+Jk).\frac{\partial X_{m}}{\partial X_{\ell}}=\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}\frac{\partial X_{k+1}}{\partial X_{k}}=\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}(I+J_{k}).

Expanding:

∏k=ℓm−1(I+Jk)\displaystyle\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}(I+J_{k}) =I+∑k=ℓm−1Jk+∑ℓ≤k1<k2<mJk1​Jk2+⋯\displaystyle=I+\sum_{k=\ell}^{m-1}J_{k}+\sum_{\ell\leq k_{1}<k_{2}<m}J_{k_{1}}J_{k_{2}}+\cdots
=I+∑k=ℓm−1Jk+O⁡(‖J‖2).\displaystyle=I+\sum_{k=\ell}^{m-1}J_{k}+O(\|J\|^{2}).

The identity matrix II appears as the leading term.

Part (iii): Direct gradient pathway.

The key structural property is that the end-to-end Jacobian contains an additive identity term:

∂Xm∂Xℓ=I+∑k=ℓm−1Jk+(higher-order terms).\frac{\partial X_{m}}{\partial X_{\ell}}=I+\sum_{k=\ell}^{m-1}J_{k}+\text{(higher-order terms)}.

This means gradients can flow directly through the residual connections without being transformed by sublayer Jacobians JkJ_{k}. For any gradient signal gg at layer mm, the gradient at layer ℓ\ell includes the term gg directly (from the II component), plus additional contributions from paths through sublayers.

In contrast, post-LN has no such additive identity: all gradient paths pass through LayerNorm Jacobians at every intermediate layer. Since JLNJ_{\LN} is projection-like (it annihilates the constant direction and contracts variance), repeated application causes exponential decay along certain directions. The pre-LN identity path avoids this compounding contraction. ∎

C.5 Proof of Theorem 5.5: Post-LN No Identity Gradient Path

Proof.

We prove each part in sequence.

Part (i): End-to-end Jacobian formula.

The post-LN layer computes Xℓ+1=LN⁡(Yℓ)X_{\ell+1}=\LN(Y_{\ell}) where Yℓ=Xℓ+MHA⁡(Xℓ)Y_{\ell}=X_{\ell}+\MHA(X_{\ell}). By the chain rule:

∂Xℓ+1∂Xℓ=JLN​(Yℓ)⋅∂Yℓ∂Xℓ=JLN​(Yℓ)⋅(I+JMHA​(Xℓ)).\frac{\partial X_{\ell+1}}{\partial X_{\ell}}=J_{\LN}(Y_{\ell})\cdot\frac{\partial Y_{\ell}}{\partial X_{\ell}}=J_{\LN}(Y_{\ell})\cdot(I+J_{\MHA}(X_{\ell})).

For ℓ<m\ell<m, chaining these derivatives:

∂Xm∂Xℓ=∏k=ℓm−1JLN​(Yk)​(I+JMHA​(Xk)).\frac{\partial X_{m}}{\partial X_{\ell}}=\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}J_{\LN}(Y_{k})(I+J_{\MHA}(X_{k})).

Part (ii): LayerNorm Jacobian is projection-like.

The LayerNorm Jacobian at y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is:

JLN​(y)=Diag⁡(γ)σ⁡(y)​(I−𝟏𝟏⊤d−(y−μ​𝟏)​(y−μ​𝟏)⊤d​σ​(y)2),J_{\LN}(y)=\frac{\Diag(\gamma)}{\sigma(y)}\left(I-\frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}}{d}-\frac{(y-\mu\mathbf{1})(y-\mu\mathbf{1})^{\top}}{d\sigma(y)^{2}}\right),

where μ=1d​∑jyj\mu=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j}y_{j} and σ2=1d​∑j(yj−μ)2+ϵ\sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j}(y_{j}-\mu)^{2}+\epsilon.

This matrix has two key properties:

  • •

    It annihilates the constant direction: JLN​(y)​𝟏=0J_{\LN}(y)\mathbf{1}=0 (from I−𝟏𝟏⊤dI-\frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}}{d}).

  • •

    It contracts variance along (y−μ​𝟏)(y-\mu\mathbf{1}).

Crucially, JLN​(y)≠I+small perturbationJ_{\LN}(y)\neq I+\text{small perturbation}; it is a genuine projection-like operator.

Part (iii): No additive identity term.

Expanding the end-to-end product:

∏k=ℓm−1JLN​(Yk)​(I+JMHA​(Xk))\displaystyle\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}J_{\LN}(Y_{k})(I+J_{\MHA}(X_{k}))
=(∏k=ℓm−1JLN​(Yk))+terms involving ​JMHA.\displaystyle\quad=\left(\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}J_{\LN}(Y_{k})\right)+\text{terms involving }J_{\MHA}.

Contrast with pre-LN where ∏k=ℓm−1(I+Jk)=I+∑kJk+⋯\prod_{k=\ell}^{m-1}(I+J_{k})=I+\sum_{k}J_{k}+\cdots. In post-LN, the leading term is ∏kJLN​(Yk)\prod_{k}J_{\LN}(Y_{k}), not II. There is no identity term because every factor is multiplied by JLN​(Yk)J_{\LN}(Y_{k}), which projects out directions.

The product of m−ℓm-\ell projection-like operators compounds: directions that are consistently projected out see exponentially decaying gradient components. ∎

Appendix D Proofs for Section 6: Training Heuristics

D.1 Proof of Theorem 6.1: Projection Scaling for Transformers

Proof.

From Theorem 5.1, the attention-pathway contribution to the MHA Lipschitz constant is:

Lattn=θ~τ⋅B¯U2⋅‖WO‖2​‖WQ‖2​‖WK‖2​‖WV‖2.L_{\mathrm{attn}}=\frac{\tilde{\theta}}{\tau}\cdot\bar{B}_{U}^{2}\cdot\|W^{O}\|_{2}\|W^{Q}\|_{2}\|W^{K}\|_{2}\|W^{V}\|_{2}.

Under the assumption ‖WQ‖2∼‖WK‖2∼‖WV‖2∼‖WO‖2∼β\|W^{Q}\|_{2}\sim\|W^{K}\|_{2}\sim\|W^{V}\|_{2}\sim\|W^{O}\|_{2}\sim\beta, this becomes:

Lattn=θ~τ⋅B¯U2⋅β4=:C0​β4,L_{\mathrm{attn}}=\frac{\tilde{\theta}}{\tau}\cdot\bar{B}_{U}^{2}\cdot\beta^{4}=:C_{0}\beta^{4},

where C0=θ~​B¯U2/τC_{0}=\tilde{\theta}\bar{B}_{U}^{2}/\tau is a positive constant independent of depth (determined by temperature, input magnitude bounds, and attention distribution geometry).

For an NN-layer network, the end-to-end Lipschitz constant involves products of per-layer Lipschitz constants. From Theorem 5.2, each pre-LN layer has Lipschitz constant bounded by (1+C1​Lattn)(1+C_{1}L_{\mathrm{attn}}) for some architectural constant C1>0C_{1}>0. The end-to-end bound is therefore:

∏ℓ=1N(1+C1​Lattn).\prod_{\ell=1}^{N}(1+C_{1}L_{\mathrm{attn}}).

We seek conditions under which this product remains bounded as N→∞N\to\infty. Using the inequality ln⁡(1+x)≤x\ln(1+x)\leq x for x>−1x>-1:

ln∏ℓ=1N(1+C1Lattn)=∑ℓ=1Nln(1+C1Lattn)≤N⋅C1Lattn.\ln\prod_{\ell=1}^{N}(1+C_{1}L_{\mathrm{attn}})=\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\ln(1+C_{1}L_{\mathrm{attn}})\leq N\cdot C_{1}L_{\mathrm{attn}}.

For the product to remain O⁡(1)O(1), we require N⋅Lattn=O⁡(1)N\cdot L_{\mathrm{attn}}=O(1), i.e., Lattn=O⁡(1/N)L_{\mathrm{attn}}=O(1/N).

Since Lattn=C0​β4L_{\mathrm{attn}}=C_{0}\beta^{4}, the condition Lattn=O⁡(1/N)L_{\mathrm{attn}}=O(1/N) requires:

β4=O(1/N)⟹β=O(N−1/4).\beta^{4}=O(1/N)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\beta=O(N^{-1/4}).

Asymmetric scaling.

If the four projections have different norms βQ,βK,βV,βO\beta_{Q},\beta_{K},\beta_{V},\beta_{O}, the condition generalizes to βQ​βK​βV​βO=O⁡(1/N)\beta_{Q}\beta_{K}\beta_{V}\beta_{O}=O(1/N), and the geometric mean (βQβKβVβO)1/4=O(N−1/4)(\beta_{Q}\beta_{K}\beta_{V}\beta_{O})^{1/4}=O(N^{-1/4}) determines the effective scaling. ∎

D.2 Proof of Theorem 6.2: Path-Length Exponent Principle

Proof.

Consider a deep network with NN layers where the dominant sensitivity pathway at each layer passes through mm linear maps. Let the operator norms at layer ℓ\ell be ‖W1(ℓ)‖2,…,‖Wm(ℓ)‖2\|W_{1}^{(\ell)}\|_{2},\ldots,\|W_{m}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}. The per-layer Lipschitz contribution from this pathway takes the form:

Sℓ=C0⋅∏j=1m‖Wj(ℓ)‖2,S_{\ell}=C_{0}\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{m}\|W_{j}^{(\ell)}\|_{2},

where C0>0C_{0}>0 is a constant capturing depth-independent factors (e.g., θ~/τ\tilde{\theta}/\tau, input magnitude bounds, nonlinearity Lipschitz constants).

Under the assumption of comparable norms ‖Wj(ℓ)‖2∼β\|W_{j}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}\sim\beta for all j∈[m]j\in[m] and ℓ∈[N]\ell\in[N]:

Sℓ=C0​βm.S_{\ell}=C_{0}\beta^{m}.

The end-to-end Lipschitz constant is bounded by the product ∏ℓ=1N(1+Sℓ)\prod_{\ell=1}^{N}(1+S_{\ell}). Taking logarithms and using ln⁡(1+x)≤x\ln(1+x)\leq x for x>0x>0:

ln∏ℓ=1N(1+Sℓ)=∑ℓ=1Nln(1+Sℓ)≤∑ℓ=1NSℓ=N⋅C0βm.\ln\prod_{\ell=1}^{N}(1+S_{\ell})=\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\ln(1+S_{\ell})\leq\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}S_{\ell}=N\cdot C_{0}\beta^{m}.

For the end-to-end Lipschitz constant to remain O⁡(1)O(1) as N→∞N\to\infty, we require N⋅βm=O⁡(1)N\cdot\beta^{m}=O(1), which yields:

βm=O(1/N)⟹β=O(N−1/m).\beta^{m}=O(1/N)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\beta=O(N^{-1/m}).

Tightness.

This scaling is tight. For the lower bound, note that ln⁡(1+x)≥x−x2/2\ln(1+x)\geq x-x^{2}/2 for x≥0x\geq 0. If Sℓ=C0​βmS_{\ell}=C_{0}\beta^{m} with β=ω(N−1/m)\beta=\omega(N^{-1/m}), then N⋅Sℓ→∞N\cdot S_{\ell}\to\infty, and the product ∏ℓ(1+Sℓ)≥exp⁡(N⋅Sℓ−N⋅Sℓ2/2)→∞\prod_{\ell}(1+S_{\ell})\geq\exp(N\cdot S_{\ell}-N\cdot S_{\ell}^{2}/2)\to\infty (since the linear term dominates for small SℓS_{\ell}). Thus β=ω(N−1/m)\beta=\omega(N^{-1/m}) leads to unbounded end-to-end sensitivity.

Asymmetric scaling.

If the mm maps have different norms β1,…,βm\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{m}, the per-layer contribution becomes Sℓ=C0​∏j=1mβjS_{\ell}=C_{0}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\beta_{j}, and the boundedness condition generalizes to:

∏j=1mβj=O⁡(1/N).\prod_{j=1}^{m}\beta_{j}=O(1/N).

The geometric mean (∏j=1mβj)1/m=O(N−1/m)\bigl(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\beta_{j}\bigr)^{1/m}=O(N^{-1/m}) determines the effective per-map scaling. ∎

Appendix E Experimental Details and Additional Results

This appendix provides full experimental details and additional results supporting Section 7.

E.1 Experimental Setup

Model architecture.

We train GPT-2-style transformers with the following configuration:

  • •

    Model dimension: d=1280d=1280

  • •

    Number of layers: N=36N=36

  • •

    Attention heads: H=20H=20

  • •

    Head dimension: dh=64d_{h}=64

  • •

    FFN hidden dimension: dff=5120d_{\text{ff}}=5120

  • •

    Context length: L=1024L=1024

  • •

    Total parameters: 774M

Training configuration.

  • •

    Optimizer: AdamW with β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95)

  • •

    Weight decay: 0.1

  • •

    Learning rate: 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} peak

  • •

    Schedule: 500-step linear warmup, cosine decay

  • •

    Batch size: 64 (micro-batch 4, gradient accumulation 16)

  • •

    Gradient clipping: norm 1.0

  • •

    Precision: bfloat16

  • •

    Hardware: NVIDIA H100 GPU

  • •

    Training steps: 5000

  • •

    Random seeds: 42, 123, 456

Data.

Models are trained on FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024), a large-scale web text corpus. We use streaming data loading with packed sequences of length 1024.

Metrics.

We track the following quantities throughout training:

  • •

    Training loss (cross-entropy)

  • •

    Gradient norm (before clipping)

  • •

    Balanced-mass factor θ⁡(p)\theta(p) estimated via greedy bisection on sampled attention distributions

  • •

    Layer-wise gradient norms

  • •

    Projection norm product Gℓ=‖WℓO‖2​‖WℓQ‖2​‖WℓK‖2​‖WℓV‖2G_{\ell}=\|W^{O}_{\ell}\|_{2}\|W^{Q}_{\ell}\|_{2}\|W^{K}_{\ell}\|_{2}\|W^{V}_{\ell}\|_{2} computed via power iteration

E.2 Theorem Verification Details

Figure 3 verifies Theorem 4.2. For small sequence lengths L∈{8,16}L\in\{8,16\}, we perform exact verification by exhaustive enumeration over all 2L2^{L} subsets. For each of 500 random logit vectors u∼𝒩⁡(0,I)u\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I):

  1. 1.

    Compute p=softmax⁡(u/τ)p=\softmax(u/\tau) with τ=1\tau=1

  2. 2.

    Compute the left-hand side: construct the Jacobian J=Diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤J=\Diag(p)-pp^{\top} and find ‖J‖∞→1\|J\|_{\infty\to 1} by exhaustive search over all sign vectors x∈{±1}Lx\in\{\pm 1\}^{L}

  3. 3.

    Compute the right-hand side: θ⁡(p)/τ\theta(p)/\tau by exhaustive search over all subsets S⊆[L]S\subseteq[L]

  4. 4.

    Record the relative error |LHS−RHS|/RHS|\text{LHS}-\text{RHS}|/\text{RHS}

For L≤16L\leq 16, the maximum relative error across all tests is below 10−1310^{-13}, consistent with double-precision floating-point arithmetic. This confirms that Theorem 4.2 is an exact equality, not merely an upper bound.

For larger L∈{32,64,128,256,512,1024}L\in\{32,64,128,256,512,1024\}, exhaustive enumeration is computationally infeasible. Instead, we use a greedy heuristic to estimate θ⁡(p)\theta(p) and verify that both sides of the identity match under this approximation.

Greedy heuristic for θ⁡(p)\theta(p).

For large LL, we estimate θ⁡(p)=4​maxS⊆[L]⁡p⁡(S)​(1−p⁡(S))\theta(p)=4\max_{S\subseteq[L]}p(S)(1-p(S)) using a greedy heuristic:

  1. 1.

    Sort probabilities in descending order: p(1)≥p(2)≥⋯≥p(L)p_{(1)}\geq p_{(2)}\geq\cdots\geq p_{(L)}

  2. 2.

    Compute cumulative sums ck=∑i=1kp(i)c_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_{(i)}

  3. 3.

    Find k∗=arg⁡mink​|ck−0.5|k^{*}=\arg\min_{k}|c_{k}-0.5|

  4. 4.

    Return θ⁡(p)≈4⋅ck∗⋅(1−ck∗)\theta(p)\approx 4\cdot c_{k^{*}}\cdot(1-c_{k^{*}})

This heuristic finds the prefix of sorted probabilities closest to mass 0.50.5. While it does not guarantee global optimality (the optimal subset may not be a prefix), it provides a tight approximation in practice. For all distributions tested with L≤16L\leq 16, the greedy heuristic matches exhaustive search exactly. The theorem’s validity rests on its algebraic proof (Appendix B), not on computational verification.

E.3 Multi-Seed Results

Table 1 shows results aggregated across 3 random seeds. Key observations:

  • •

    Pre-LN achieves 16% lower final loss than Post-LN

  • •

    Pre-LN has much tighter variance (±0.01\pm 0.01) compared to Post-LN (±0.45\pm 0.45)

  • •

    Pre-LN experiences zero gradient spikes; Post-LN averages 0.3 spikes per run

  • •

    Both architectures maintain θ/τ=1.0\theta/\tau=1.0 at the end of training

E.4 Layer-wise θ⁡(p)\theta(p) Analysis

Figure 4 shows that θ⁡(p)≈1\theta(p)\approx 1 holds across all layers, not just at the output. We sample attention distributions from layers 0 (first), 18 (middle), and 35 (last) and compute θ⁡(p)\theta(p) for each. Both Pre-LN and Post-LN show θ≈1.0\theta\approx 1.0 uniformly.

This confirms that the persistence of maximal softmax sensitivity is a global property of trained transformers, not an artifact of measuring only the final layer.

E.5 Sensitivity Proxy Analysis

Figure 5 tracks the full sensitivity proxy Sℓ=(θ/τ)⋅B¯ℓ2⋅GℓS_{\ell}=(\theta/\tau)\cdot\bar{B}_{\ell}^{2}\cdot G_{\ell} throughout training. Key observations:

  • •

    Pre-LN has higher absolute SℓS_{\ell} values (median ∼105\sim 10^{5}) compared to Post-LN (median ∼103\sim 10^{3})

  • •

    Despite higher sensitivity, Pre-LN remains stable due to the identity gradient path

  • •

    Pre-LN shows higher coefficient of variation (CV ≈0.97\approx 0.97) across layers compared to Post-LN (CV ≈0.40\approx 0.40)

This reveals why Pre-LN tolerates higher raw sensitivity: the residual structure controls how sensitivity compounds across depth.

Figure 6 shows the layer-wise distribution of SℓS_{\ell} at the end of training:

  • •

    Pre-LN: SℓS_{\ell} grows monotonically with layer depth, reaching maximum at the final layer

  • •

    Post-LN: SℓS_{\ell} is relatively flat across layers 1–35, with a spike only at the output layer

The monotonic growth in Pre-LN reflects the accumulation of residual stream magnitude B¯ℓ\bar{B}_{\ell} across depth, which is controlled by the identity gradient path. The flat profile in Post-LN reflects the magnitude reset from LayerNorm at each layer.

E.6 Factor Attribution

To understand which factors drive sensitivity changes, we decompose in log space:

log⁡Sℓ=log⁡(θ/τ)+2​log⁡B¯ℓ+log⁡Gℓ.\log S_{\ell}=\log(\theta/\tau)+2\log\bar{B}_{\ell}+\log G_{\ell}.

Since θ/τ≈1\theta/\tau\approx 1 throughout training, we have log⁡(θ/τ)≈0\log(\theta/\tau)\approx 0, and the relevant decomposition is between GℓG_{\ell} (projection norms) and B¯ℓ\bar{B}_{\ell} (hidden state magnitudes).

Pre-LN factor attribution.

  • •

    Change in log⁡Gℓ\log G_{\ell}: Δ​log⁡G≈1.29\Delta\log G\approx 1.29

  • •

    Change in log⁡B¯ℓ2\log\bar{B}_{\ell}^{2}: Δ​log⁡B¯2≈2.91\Delta\log\bar{B}^{2}\approx 2.91

  • •

    Hidden state magnitudes are the dominant driver of sensitivity growth

Post-LN factor attribution.

  • •

    Change in log⁡Gℓ\log G_{\ell}: Δ​log⁡G≈1.13\Delta\log G\approx 1.13

  • •

    Change in log⁡B¯ℓ2\log\bar{B}_{\ell}^{2}: Δ​log⁡B¯2≈0\Delta\log\bar{B}^{2}\approx 0

  • •

    Hidden states remain controlled by output LayerNorm; only GℓG_{\ell} grows

This reveals a key difference: in Pre-LN, hidden state magnitudes grow substantially but this is tolerated due to the identity gradient path. In Post-LN, hidden states are controlled by LayerNorm, but the gradient pathology from LayerNorm Jacobian products still causes instability.
